messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Mateo Rodriguez, a man of sixty-two with a lifetime dedicated to the expressive power of dance, now moved through his days with a quiet, unsettling vigilance. The traumatic event that shattered his world had been a motor vehicle collision, a life-threatening incident that left him physically bruised but emotionally fractured. He had been a passenger when their car was struck violently from the side, sending it spinning into a concrete barrier. Trapped in the mangled wreckage, he remembered the horrifying screech of tearing metal, the deafening shatter of glass, and the frantic shouts that seemed to swirl around him as he lay utterly helpless. The sensation of being violently jostled, followed by the terrifying pressure of the crushed vehicle, was seared into his memory. Even the touch of the paramedics, though meant to save him, had felt sudden, invasive, and alarming as they worked to free him.

Now, when Mateo tried to articulate the experience, he often found himself grasping for words, shaking his head with a frustrated sigh. "It's not... I can't explain it," he would say, his hands making vague, helpless gestures, unable to put the chaotic horror into a coherent narrative. Yet, the sounds were vividly present; the screech of tires and the splintering crash often erupted in his mind, sharp and sudden, as if happening anew. With these auditory recalls came an intense shame, a burning sensation that coiled in his gut. He had come to believe, deep down, that "the event happened to me because of the sort of person I am," a cruel self-blame that he couldn't logically justify but couldn't shake either. This belief was compounded by a pervasive sense of "I can't stop bad things from happening to me," leaving him feeling utterly powerless against the world's cruelties. What frightened Mateo most, however, was the conviction that "I will never be able to feel normal emotions again." The vibrant joy he once found in his art, the tender connection with his wife, Elena, now felt distant, muted, like a forgotten melody.

This pervasive sense of threat permeated his daily life. Every time he entered a room or building, his eyes automatically darted around, "scanning for exits," a compulsive habit born from the terror of being trapped. This made his work at the dance studio particularly challenging; his focus was often split, his body tense, rather than fluidly engaged with the space. More acutely, any unexpected physical contact sent a jolt of pure alarm through him. A hand on his shoulder from a fellow dancer, Elena's gentle touch as she passed him in their kitchen – these innocent gestures triggered an immediate startle, a surge of adrenaline, and a rush of "negative emotions" like fear or even a flash of irrational anger.

To cope with the relentless intrusion of memories and the overwhelming feelings, Mateo had developed several maladaptive strategies. When the shame or horror became too intense, he would "deliberately try to leave my body or blank out," retreating into a detached state that offered temporary relief but left him feeling even more disconnected. He also "tried hard not to think about the trauma," pushing the thoughts away with fierce concentration, often immersing himself in the intricate footwork of a dance routine until his mind was too exhausted to wander. Yet, the quiet hours of the night offered little respite. Fearing the vivid nightmares or simply the solitude that allowed intrusive thoughts to surface, he would "stay up until very late," watching old movies or reading, anything to delay the inevitable darkness of sleep.

These changes had accumulated over the past year, casting a long shadow over his life. His emotional distance strained his cherished relationship with Elena, who often found herself bewildered by his sudden withdrawals. Professionally, his "startle to touch" made partner work, a cornerstone of his dance style, increasingly difficult and awkward, leading to him subtly avoiding certain rehearsals or performances. The once expressive and connected dancer now felt like a prisoner in his own body, his art diminished, his passion dulled. It was Elena, observing his increasing isolation and the deep sadness that settled in his eyes, who gently urged him to seek help. Mateo, exhausted by the constant vigilance, the emotional numbness, and the pervasive shame, finally agreed, clinging to a fragile hope that he might yet find a way back to the man he once was, to feel the music, and to move freely through a world that no longer felt so dangerous.
